processing: Orthodox black tea made in a small old factory: withered, rolled, sieved, oxidised, dried, cleaned of fibre and graded, with no CTC.
harvest_season: Picking dates are not well documented; as in other South Indian hill gardens, tea is grown across much of the year.
appearance_dry: Dark, fairly small orthodox leaf, as is typical of South Indian high-grown tea.
appearance_liquor: Clear reddish-amber, typically lighter than an Assam.
taste_profile: Described as fresh from the altitude and also as robust; a brisk, clean cup is what to expect from high-grown South Indian black tea.

brewing.notes: Western-style. Start shorter than you would with Assam, as high-grown tea of this kind can turn sharp.

vintage_note: Mostly sold or bought at the estate itself, often to visitors, and rarely with detailed lot data. Treat it like other South Indian orthodox black tea: buy the freshest you can and drink within a year or two.
description:
Kolukkumalai is the tea estate above Munnar that is famous for one thing: its height. At about 2,170 metres it is celebrated as the highest tea plantation in the world, though some accounts give a higher figure. It lies in Theni district in Tamil Nadu, even though the jeep road up starts from the Kerala side at Suryanelli.

The tea is made the old way, in a small factory using the orthodox method rather than CTC. Visitors can watch the steps, which is a large part of the estate's fame.

Descriptions of the cup are short and rather general: fresh from the altitude, sometimes robust. Beyond that it is fair to expect what is typical of high-grown South Indian black tea, a clean, brisk cup that is lighter than an Assam. Steep it a little shorter and taste before adding milk.

Most people meet this tea on a trip, as a packet from the estate. If you buy one there, ask when it was made, since that matters more than the slogan on the box.
history:
The small factory is said to date from the 1930s, built under the British, and travel accounts note that it still works with old machinery and wooden interiors. Some give 1930 exactly, and one puts the estate's first planting in the early 1900s, but these are tourism sources and the exact dates are not firm.

The highest-in-the-world claim is repeated widely, including in the tea trade press, and it has made the estate a jeep-safari destination from Munnar.
